niche.habitat: Tidal flats, shallow sea edges, and fog-damp meadow slopes.
niche.diet: Aquatic greens, soft grasses, and mineral-rich algae.
niche.active: Diurnal; peaks at dawn fog and shifting tides.

body: Stilt-wading legs with splayed toes distribute weight across soft tidal mud, preventing sinkage in 1.6-bar dense air. A braced, flexible neck and spear-strike beak allow rapid, low-energy plucking without torso bending, conserving stamina for quick escapes.

links: Splayed toes spread weight on soft mud

skill.effect: The creature strides effortlessly across shallow water and thick mud without tiring. You can safely follow it through wetlands.

chains.weakness: Spring tides flood the flats; catch it at high water.

plausibility.summary: Semi-diurnal shelf tides (F13), not a strict twice-daily mudflat clock on a 26 h day—tie exposure to tide phase in UI. Cap Stilt Wade at ~1.2–1.5 m/s in knee-deep mud or soft peat; reserve 2 m/s for firm sand/causeway (F4: dense air makes fast wading costlier than the skill implies).
fixes: Semi-diurnal shelf tides (F13), not a strict twice-daily mudflat clock on a 26 h day—tie exposure to tide phase in UI. Cap Stilt Wade at ~1.2–1.5 m/s in knee-deep mud or soft peat; reserve 2 m/s for firm sand/causeway (F4: dense air makes fast wading costlier than the skill implies).

analogues.organism: Black-winged stilt (Himantopus himantopus) and American flamingo (Phoenicopterus ruber): long legs for shallow inundation, broad-footed weight spreading on soft substrate (standard wading-bird limb ecology; textbook-level, unverified author/year).
analogues.mechanism: as named by the judge; no mechanism or reference recorded

chains.trait: Long, flexible neck for surface viewing
links: Long neck lifts eyes above the surface

skill.effect: It raises its long neck to peer over reeds and water, strongly spotting hidden creatures. You can notice concealed threats that would otherwise go unnoticed.

chains.weakness: Wind pushes the neck; gusts above 8m/s force it down for 5s.

journal.en: It watches the water from above the water.

analogues.organism: Anhinga / darter (Anhinga spp.): body submerged in turbid water, neck as periscope for surface vision and aim (Johnsgard, C. A. 1993, *Cormorants, Darters, and Pelicans of the World*—from memory, unverified). Wind weakness matches F19 (1.6× wind load on a long lever).
analogues.mechanism: as named by the judge; no mechanism or reference recorded

links: A strike from above needs reach, not pursuit
A miss tangles the long neck

skill.effect: It lunges forward with a sharp beak strike at nearby targets. If it misses, it remains exposed for a short while before recovering its stance.

chains.weakness: Bait two misses; the neck tangles and it cannot strike for 4s.

journal.en: It fishes by stabbing the cloud.

plausibility.summary: In F20 turbidity, prey must be within ~0.5 m of the surface (ripples, fin breaks); subsurface fish are strike targets only after Periscope cues, not deep pursuit. Keep miss/recoil penalties—they match real heron strike overshoot and recovery lag.
fixes: In F20 turbidity, prey must be within ~0.5 m of the surface (ripples, fin breaks); subsurface fish are strike targets only after Periscope cues, not deep pursuit. Keep miss/recoil penalties—they match real heron strike overshoot and recovery lag.

analogues.organism: Great blue heron (Ardea herodias) and goliath heron (Ardea goliath): downward spear-strike on sighted or rippling prey in murky shallows (Kushlan & Hancock 2005, *Herons*—from memory, unverified).
analogues.mechanism: as named by the judge; no mechanism or reference recorded

links: Drag on neck selects for bracing
1.6 bar air density loads neck structure

skill.effect: Range grab; pull enemy close or break their stance.

chains.weakness: Neck vulnerable to direct bite if caught.

journal.en: A heron of stone and sinew. The neck is a whip. High wind breaks weak necks; he stands.

plausibility.summary: Split selection story: S-curve locking and myofascial bracing primarily resist F19 gusts and strike recoil; 1.6 bar air (F4) raises aerodynamic drag on an extended neck but is secondary to wind on exposed coast. Drop or relocate 'high foliage feeding' journal beat—or make it rare dry-season browse so the neck isn't both heron-periscope and giraffe-browser in one chain.
fixes: Split selection story: S-curve locking and myofascial bracing primarily resist F19 gusts and strike recoil; 1.6 bar air (F4) raises aerodynamic drag on an extended neck but is secondary to wind on exposed coast. Drop or relocate 'high foliage feeding' journal beat—or make it rare dry-season browse so the neck isn't both heron-periscope and giraffe-browser in one chain.

analogues.organism: Heron cervical musculature and double S-curve lock during strike (Bout, R. G. 1984, neck myology in birds—from memory, unverified); convergent long-neck support also in giraffe but for browsing, not wading (different mechanism).
analogues.mechanism: as named by the judge; no mechanism or reference recorded

temperament: Timid herd-dweller that uses height and early warning to avoid confrontation.
moments: Dawn mist parts; the herd lifts its necks in unison, scanning the fog line. A sudden stampede kicks up salt spray as a shadow crosses the causeway.
